speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege. It arises out of an article appearing in the Globe and Mail. I wish to show no disrespect to the Globe and Mail; however, in this article I am listed as one of the members who were absent on a certain vote. On that occasion I was paired, as I pointed out in the house on a number of occasions, with the hon. member for Verdun (Mr. Mackasey), who was one of the delegates to the United Nations. I believe this delegation was appointed by the Prime Minister of this country to conduct very important business at the United Nations. I was here at the building at all times during that vote and during those proceedings. This is my point of privilege. I think it affects myself and the other hon. member. I have always believed one of the most important aspects of a person's character is to keep his word. 1 believe when a man has given his word to someone, other things should not interfere with the keeping of it.

speechtext: Will the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation take advantage of the facilities of the national film board as recommended in the report of the Glassco commission and, if so, (a) when will such arrangement commence (b) will such an arrangement minimize the capital program of the C.B.C., and (c) will the national film board be enabled to contract out additional work to private producers as a consequence?

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: C.B.C. USE OF FILM BOARD FACILITIES
speechtext:
(a) The Canadian Broadcasting Corporation has for some years made extensive use of the production facilities of the national film board. The board has been one of the major suppliers of film programs to the corporation. Liaison practices between the two organizations ensure that activities

are reviewed on both policy and working levels. The effectiveness of liaison is receiving careful attention.
(b)	It is unlikely that further utilization of the board's facilities would have an appreciable effect on the corporation's capital program because expenditures for film production equipment represent only a small fraction of the total capital cost involved.
(c)	The national film board's policy is to utilize its facilities at the economic operating level. Should the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation increase its requirements from the national film board significantly, it could result in the board increasing the amount of work tendered to private film companies.

1.	Is the government giving consideration to the abolition of welfare categories, and their replacement by a provincial-federal welfare system that would provide aid on the basis of need?

speakerposition: Minister of Amateur Sport; Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
1. The federal government's position on the whole field of public assistance, including the categorical aid programs for the aged, the blind and the disabled, is being carefully studied in the Department of National Health and Welfare, and an interdepartmental committee is developing specific proposals in this area. During the federal-provincial conference on September 9 and 10 there was discussion of public assistance programs in which some criticism of the categorical approach was voiced and support for a broader type of assistance program was expressed. The communique agreed to at the meeting suggested "that the whole field of social assistance should be jointly re-examined, in the hope of developing one general assistance program based on need". It is expected that this question will be further considered at the federal-provincial conference in November.
2. Under the three categorical programs, aid is provided on the basis of a means test .taking into account income and assets, with

specific age and residence requirements and maximum benefits and, in the case of two of the programs, with provision for precise tests of blindness or permanent and total disability. While these characteristics of the programs result in some rigidity, the programs have the value of being clearly defined and understood and continue to fill an important role in supporting the groups for which they are intended. In some high cost areas however the benefits provided through these programs have not been adequate for all recipients and this has led to the development of measures of supplementary aid. There has also been some feeling that more positive steps should be taken to help persons who fall outside these programs, among them those with disabilities which cannot be viewed as permanent and total but which may prevent employment. The provinces have also indicated an interest in having more flexibility in developing programs suited to their particular local needs.
3.	See answer 1, above. The categorical assistance programs have been developed over the years in collaboration with the provinces, and any modification in them would need to be worked out co-operatively. It is hoped that the basis for detailed federal-provincial discussions on this matter will be laid at the federal-provincial conference next month.

subtopic: PROTECTION AGAINST FOOD POISONING FROM FISH PRODUCTS

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Hon. H. J. Robichaud (Minister of Fisheries):
subtopic: PROTECTION AGAINST FOOD POISONING FROM FISH PRODUCTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, yesterday the hon. member for Queens asked me a question in connection with a warning by the United States food and drug administration that some smoked fish products from the great lakes contain the botulus organism, and I promised I would give a full reply today.
The Departments of National Health and Welfare and Fisheries have viewed with concern the recent evidence from the United States associating death from botulism with the consumption of specific types of smoked fish. During the past three years nine deaths and a number of non-fatal cases of illness have been shown to be due to the presence in the smoked fish of a toxic substance produced by a bacterium called Clostridium botulinum type E. No reports of similar illness have occurred in Canada during this period.
Canadian consumers should be informed that cooking destroys the toxic substance.

Therefore any food product eaten immediately after thorough cooking is safe with regard to this type of poisoning. Investigators of the two departments have had this problem under study for about two years. There is evidence to suggest that the practice of packing smoked fish in impermeable plastic wrappers increases the risk of botulism from this product. Accordingly the two departments are considering legislation to prohibit the sale of smoked fish packed in containers sealed to exclude air unless the packaged product has been rendered commercially sterile by a suitable heat process.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Prime Minister.
Yesterday, on St. Helen's island, the 1967 world fair flag was hoisted up; could the right hon. gentleman assure us that Canada will have a truly Canadian flag on the occasion of this exhibition?

Righl Hon. L. B. Pearson (Prime Minister):
Yes, Mr. Speaker, I am glad to give that assurance.
The house resumed, from Friday, October 25, consideration of the motion of Mr. Gordon for second reading of Bill No. C-95, to amend the Income Tax Act.

Mr. Speaker to say the least an omnibus bill such as this has a great many things in it, but this afternoon I would like to spend my time dealing with those aspects which are connected with the Department of Industry. I refer to those parts which propose certain tax advantages and exemptions for the areas designated in the recent legislation concerning the Department of Industry.

Income Tax Act
I would like to make it quite clear that I believe every member of the house is thoroughly in agreement with the good intentions of this legislation and the general principles behind it, but there are many hon. members, myself included, who take considerable exception to the methods used to attain these objectives and to the manner in which the legislation has been introduced.
Our objections and criticisms can be divided into two general categories. First, there is gross interference with provincial rights; and second, the methods used and the statistical formulae applied leave much to be desired and have resulted in some thoroughly ridiculous situations.
I shall deal first with the question of interference in provincial affairs. Ever since our country became an independent nation in 1867, from time to time its constitution has been open to considerable question with respect to rights vis-a-vis the federal government and the provinces. I agree it is sometimes difficult for even the most acute legal minds in this country to determine with any degree of accuracy which fields lie within the authority of the provinces and which lie within the authority of the federal government. When these matters are brought before the courts and, ultimately, before the Supreme Court of Canada, a decision is made. The first point I should like to make in this regard and I have discussed this matter with others, in this house and elsewhere, who have had considerable legal experience, is that it would seem to me that the government should take a careful second look at these clauses of Bill C-95, because it would seem that a good case could be made for the contention that they are ultra vires.
I do not wish to engage in a legal argument at this time. Indeed, it would be improper to do so, because any legal argument presented here would be a matter of opinion; it would be up to the courts to decide whether or not such arguments are valid. However, the reasoning behind my contention is that, by giving certain tax reliefs and exemptions to certain areas the relevant clauses of this bill are, directing the location of property, namely land and capital, within certain specific areas of the country in the provinces. The legislation may well be tested in the courts and I think the government should take a most careful look at these provisions before the measure leaves this house. An ounce of prevention, as the saying goes, is worth a pound of cure. Perhaps appropriate changes and amendments could be made as a result of a further examination by the law officers of the crown.
Let us assume, however, that this legislation is intra vires and will stand the test

of the courts. It is clear it is interfering in fields which normally belong to the provinces. There has certainly been no consultation with provincial authorities with respect to this lgislation. There is ample evidence to support this assertion. For instance, the premier of British Columbia objected violently to his own home town of Kelowna being referred to as a depressed area, and the municipal officials of other places including Brantford, in the first instance, have objected to their areas being designated without consultation. So here we have a government, which has talked so much about "co-operative confederation," setting what does not appear to be a good example by putting forward, in the absence of consultation, legislation which clearly affects provincial responsibilities.
There is another point which might be raised in this connection. I know that the province of Ontario has prevented a price war, so to speak, between municipalities bidding for new industries. I suspect other provinces have enacted similar legislation. I know it has been the practice in the past for some municipalities to offer tax concessions to new industries such as free utilities, or utilities at a reduced rate, for a number of years; tax reductions, and the like. This practice has been prohibited by the province of Ontario and, no doubt, by other provinces. Legislation of the kind now being imposed by the federal government without consultation negates this principle and detracts from the usefulness of the measures taken by the government of Ontario and, as I have suggested, by other provinces. This is a field which has so far been left to the provinces, and the amendments we are considering represent an invasion of that field by the federal government.
The idea behind legislation of this type is a good one. If the minister and those responsible for this bill had consulted with the provinces, the difficulty to which I have referred might have been circumvented and the ground for the objections I am raising might not exist. But this was not done, and I would hope that in future it will be done before legislation such as this is applied.
Another question which arises is that of duplication. Most of the provinces have highly developed departments of industry and economic development. They have done a great deal to help themselves. I have more knowledge of the situation in the province of Ontario than I have of developments in other provinces, but in Ontario a great deal has been done to encourage industry to enter the province. Directorates, with staffs of civil servants and experts, have been set up for this purpose. What do we find in this Department of Industry? I have here a document

put out by the department for the purpose of recruiting staff. It looks like Parkinson's law gone mad. There is clearly going to be immense duplication of effort in putting into practice the amendment proposed to the act and it seems to me the government would be better advised to use this department as a co-ordinating instrument and, perhaps, as a means of assisting financially the province in this field, instead of duplicating work which the provinces are already doing.
Another question occurs to me. Why did the government bring in legislation such as this without consulting the provinces and, through them, the municipalities? I think the answer will be found in some remarks which were made in this house a short while ago by my hon. friend from Brome-Missisquoi (Mr. Grafftey) when he very ably pointed out that the occupants of the treasury benches seem to have certain functions of government mixed up. As I recall his observations, my hon. friend referred to one of Mr. Burke's essays on government, an essay which pointed out the necessity of divorcing the legislative function of government from the administrative. Those engaged in discharging the legislative function of government are elected representatives accustomed to consultation and to dealing at first hand with members of the public. Those in the administrative branch, on the other hand, have the task of carrying out the legislative proposals and they are accustomed to doing so in a somewhat peremptory way. It may not be coincidence that a large percentage of the present cabinet-I think it is about one third-* is composed of those who do, in fact, have an administrative background-some people might refer to it as a bureaucratic background. It depends, of course, on what one means by these various words but it remains true that a large number of the most important cabinet posts are now held by people who have an administrative or quasi-administrative background. As a result, one finds this kind of thinking: we know what is good for you; we are not interested in consulting people at a lower level; we are imposing this on you from on high. The Minister of Industry (Mr. Drury) whose department is the most closely related to these clauses under consideration is, admittedly, a little different from those who are normally thought of as being bureaucrats. Nevertheless, he has an administrative background and I have heard some people refer to him as a "gold-plated bureaucrat". He has this background and this manner of thinking. That is why we can expect not only legislation of the type now before us, but more of it in the future.
Another main heading under which I group these objections to the relevant clauses of
Income Tax Act
Bill C-95 concern the method used to designate those areas which are to receive tax relief. A great deal has been said about this in the house already by members on both sides, and a great many statistics have been produced. Most hon. members who have had any association with statistics-and I am sure the hon. gentleman is among them'-know that statistics can be selected to suit the particular results which are required.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The Minister of Agriculture says they are for losers.

He may well be right. Anyway, we have all heard the story about the statistician six feet tall who was drowned in a river which had an average depth of three feet. I think some of the statistics used in the designation of these areas might come within the compass of that little anecdote. I do not wish to discuss the formula used by the Department of Industry in designating these areas at great length, but I think it is fair to say that some sort of arithmetical average was used in arriving at these figures and that special circumstances such as arise in the now famous case of the city of Brantford were, clearly, not taken into account. The hon. member for Northumberland (Miss Jewett) stated in the course of the speech she made in this house recently that in her opinion the government has adopted a reasonably good method of designating these areas by using statistics of growth and unemployment over a period of time. Referring to similar circumstances in countries outside Canada, she said the real issue in those other countries did not concern the criteria used but the question of how large the areas should be. I have pointed out that the statistical formula which the government has adopted leaves much to be desired because it does not allow for aberrations or unusual circumstances. I think it would have been preferable if a more complex formula had been adopted capable of taking such circumstances into account. But the main issue, as indicated by the hon. member for Northumberland, is to the size of the areas chosen. It was decided, apparently, that the areas covered by national employment offices would be considered as areas which could be designated as areas to receive special assistance. On the face of it, that appears to be a logical way in which to proceed, especially as statistics of unemployment and economic growth over a period of time are the basis for designating these areas. However, I believe there are serious objections to the practical application of this method of procedure.
Let us consider, for example, a large metropolitan area such as Toronto. I drive to

Income Tax Act
Toronto almost every week end and I think it is 24 or 25 miles from one end of the metropolitan area to the other. I do not suppose the government would contemplate for one moment suggesting that if the rate of growth in the east end of Toronto was less rapid than in the west end, special concessions should be given to industry to locate in that part of the metropolitan area which was not progressing as fast as the other. Yet, apparently, this is what has happened in the case of Brantford. The cities of Galt, Guelph, Brantford, Woodstock and Kitchener form part of the same industrial complex in the area concerned, an area of just about the same size as Toronto or Montreal. Merely because it so happened that there were separate national employment offices in these various cities, it was decided it would be possible to designate one city while passing over another. I can tell the hon. gentleman that labour flows freely between these various industrial cities. A great many people who work in one large factory in my own city come from Brantford. Many people in my own district work in Kitchener. The distances involved are not nearly as great as they are between one end of Toronto and the other.
In fact, this whole area is an industrial complex itself and its cities and towns are rapidly growing closer and closer together. I say that this would not apply to places like Windsor, Elliot Lake or Cornwall and other areas which have been designated. These towns are well removed from other industrial centres, and I do not think anyone can find any objection, except the one I pointed out in the first part of my remarks, to these places being designated. But when you take one part of what is essentially one industrial complex and single it out for preference as opposed to the other parts, I find it very offensive and unreasonable.
I realize the government has put itself in a rather difficult position; I think all hon. members realize this. The city of Brantford was designated an area to receive assistance, and it is indeed difficult for the government to repeal this decision. Any reasonable hon. member would accept that. But there is something else the government can do to help matters, and that is this. Since I have pointed out that this whole area of Galt, Guelph, Kitchener, Woodstock, Waterloo, and so on, is all part of the same industrial complex, to make things a little fairer the government could very well designate the whole area as one to receive these tax advantages. In addition to incidentally helping the growth of the

area it would certainly do a great deal to disperse industry, instead of its locating constantly in the city of Toronto, which as many people have pointed out is perhaps a socially undesirable thing. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Gordon) looks a little shocked at that, but I think we have all heard hon. members from his side of the house in the past say that it is probably a good thing to disperse industry so that cities do not get bigger and bigger while other places do not grow at all. I do not think the minister will disagree with that. I have no objection to the city of Toronto. I am very fond of it; I received part of my education there, and I like the city and its people. But I think he could hardly object to the proposition that it is socially desirable to prevent a city from getting too large, a condition which breeds all sorts of undesirable things.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Would the hon. member permit a question from one who happens to come from Toronto. I am sure he did not mean to imply that it was socially undesirable for people to live in Toronto, did he?

That all depends, Mr. Speaker, on what one might think was socially undesirable. Perhaps I have been misunderstood, but what I meant was that I think it is socially undesirable in any province to have one city become increasingly large with a heavy concentration of population in one area, which leads to a number of social evils which you do not get in smaller places.
There are those who have been unkind enough to point out that they think certain municipalities have been discriminated against, and this is attributed mostly to governments. I have heard it suggested in a very unkind way that the special designation of Brantford was a rather refined method of political patronage, in view of the political representation of Brantford. I do not think I can agree with that because I am sure that is not the case. From what we have heard lately in this house I do not think the government could ever be accused of refined political patronage in view of the crude methods we have recently heard of. I think that disposes of that argument.
I should like to deal with some remarks made by the Minister of Industry (Mr. Drury) when he replied to a question from me, concerning unemployment in the city of Brantford, during the course of debate on a previous occasion. I pointed out that because of the relocation of the Massey-Ferguson plant at Brantford, which is perhaps the principal industry in Brantford, there had been a large amount of temporary unemployment.

This point was also made by other members. The minister replied, as reported on page 3652 of Hansard for October 16:
The figures I have given to the house related to the current summer months while this high level, or allegedly high level, of construction activity has been going on in Brantford. When these buildings are completed those in the construction trades engaged in building the plants will be laid off. They will be replaced by the people operating these plants, but there will still be the same number displaced in the unemployment roles as those now engaged in the construction industry and who will be laid off when building is completed.
I thought there was something a little peculiar about that so I took the trouble to look into the matter, and I found that the Massey-Ferguson plant at Brantford is being built by a very large Toronto firm. It is an international firm which has a Canadian connection in Toronto called Cunningham-Limp, a hyphenated name. About 90 per cent of those employed in building the plant come from Toronto, so I do not think there will likely be many from Brantford laid off when the job is completed, or an increase of the unemployment roll for the city of Brantford.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, it is no use making a purely critical speech in the house unless one tries to offer something constructive in exchange. In summary therefore I suggest this: I hope the government, when it deals with matters such as this in the future, matters which clearly interfere with provincial fields, will consult the provinces and/or the municipalities concerned before it adopts this legislation. Before any more of these areas are designated to receive tax advantages I hope they will be consulted. As I said in the first place, we approve of this legislation; I think everyone does. But it is the methods used to bring it into effect which are under criticism.
Second, I hope the government will have a good look at Bill No. C-95, as to the possibility of its being ultra vires. Then I would also suggest a very careful look be given at the method of designating these areas. The hon. member for Northumberland (Miss Jewett) made a very able speech in this connection and pointed out ways in which the legislation could be improved. I hope her remarks will be given consideration.
Finally, because of the big row which has been so widely publicized all over Canada in connection with the designation of Brantford, I hope the minister in question will very carefully look at the whole industrial area surrounding that city. While it may be technically a series of areas, through the use of the national employment office as a base for designating an area I would ask the minister to look at the actual facts of the matter and
Income Tax Act
to designate the whole complex, of which Brantford is but a part. As I have already mentioned, it would include Kitchener, Guelph, Woodstock, Waterloo and the like. I think this would obviate some of the difficulties which have arisen. I shall probably have some more remarks to make when we get to a clause by clause study of the bill in committee. I realize I have wandered a little far afield, but since this bill is so closely related to the Department of Industry and covers so many matters I felt I was entitled to do so.

Mr. Speaker, it is with pleasure that I rise to speak on Bill C-95, an act to amend the Income Tax Act.
I only wish to point out to the house the discrimination which may result within some categories of people from that all too well known Income Tax Act. The small wage earners, who cannot afford to hire an accountant to prepare their income tax returns, are those who are confronted with that all too well known problem, that all too well known return which comes at the beginning of the year.
I have here a letter from one of my constituents who is quite surprised that the Minister of National Revenue should send him a letter to tell him that his claim for charitable donations has been reduced to $200. That man is amazed at such a thing, and he tells me that he will not go and see at the Quebec office what it is all about because he thinks it is useless and he asks me what to do. The employees of the income tax office tell him that they have the right to do so and that everything is according to regulations.
In my opinion, an investigation should be made and those people told why supposedly genuine receipts for charitable donations are reduced from $400 to $200. In this case, Mr. Claude Cote, residing at 586 Napoleon street, Quebec city, will get a reimbursement of only $13.15 instead of $45. Several other people are in the same situation.
Mr. Speaker, in my riding, small businessmen, small shopkeepers struggle with their income tax return at the beginning of each year and they cannot even afford to hire an accountant, and even if they do, it is at the price of great sacrifices. And why is that? Simply because that income tax form is too complicated and not easily understood by most people. In fact, nine people out of ten cannot understand the terminology of those famous forms.
I saw yesterday in the Montreal La Presse that the arts faculty students at the University of Montreal and the night students at Sir

Income Tax Act
George Williams University have signified their intention of meeting the parliamentary secretary of the federal minister to ask that their education costs be deductible. At the present time, regular students only are entitled to that privilege. Students of the arts faculty of the university of Montreal and those taking evening courses in any university are not considered then to be regular students by the government. In my opinion, they should be entitled to such a reduction. I would even go as far as to say that family heads should be allowed to deduct from their income tax all it costs them today to educate their children.
It is my considered opinion that the Income Tax Act should be revised and simplified in order that it may be understood by all Canadian citizens who have to deal with this famous problem of the income tax return.
It is the lower bracket salaried workers who are unfairly treated in this, because they have to fill their returns as best they can, since they do not understand all the wording and cannot afford the advice of those experts who always find a way to reduce the tax to a minimum. What is then to be feared in all that? I believe that the victim is always the low salaried worker, the small concern or the small merchant.
If the return forms were simplified there would be much less trouble for the general public, which has nothing but hate and contempt for the Minister of National Revenue. It is precisely because of the complexity and ambiguity of the Income Tax Act that the minister's experts should, in my opinion, try to simplify the language used in income tax returns.
If we had clear, simple and precise return forms that anyone could understand and if the expressions used were more familiar, all Canadians would be proud, at the beginning of the year, to pay what they owe to the government. As it is, the prospect of having to fill out a return in the near future is a nightmare.
Therefore, I feel that it would be possible to avoid such a headache for our constituents by simplifying the Income Tax Act.
Mr. Speaker, as representatives of the people, our duty here is to approve good legislation and fight bad legislation, but especially to improve legislation which needs to be improved and the Income Tax Act is certainly one which could stand improvement.
I feel that all members will support the amendment I wish to bring to this bill in order, once again, to be fair to the small wage earners of Canada and especially those of my riding, where the great majority of people belong to the working class and, all
[Mr. Plourde.l
things considered, find it hard to earn a living and have to work both in the daytime and in the evening to make ends meet. And why? To keep our largest industry, the federal government, going.
I move, seconded by the hon. member for Charlevoix (Mr. Belanger) that Bill C-95 be not now read a second time but that it be resolved that, in the opinion of this house, the said bill should be redrafted by the counsels, advisers, experts, translators and drafters of the Department of Finance with a view to clarifying, elucidating, explicating, vulgarizing, clearing up, explaining and bringing within the understanding of all concerned the provisions of the said bill, so as to improve the terminology, the lexicology, the phraseology and the punctuation thereof in order to avoid the complications, entanglements, uncertainties and ambiguities which tend to render the Department of National Revenue odious, despicable, despised and held in contempt by the public.
I hope, Mr. Speaker, that the members of the house will be happy to adopt that amendment.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. W. Pickersgill (Secretary of Stale):
speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I am wondering if this is an amendment or a dictionary. I am wondering also if that amendment is in order. I submit to Your Honour that it is urgent to decide whether it is or not.

Mr. Speaker, on the point of order. If the Secretary of State (Mr. Pickersgill), whose knowledge of the procedure is well known, is only wondering if the proposed amendment is in order, I claim that it is.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I might say that offhand the proposed amendment would appear to be anticipating the committee stage, where it is possible to suggest that certain changes be made by way of amendment to a bill before the committee; but if any hon. member has any comments to make before I make a formal ruling I would be pleased to hear him on the point of order.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, because I do not want to encourage amendments at any stage I had hesitated to suggest that what is sought to be done by officials outside the house would be a more appropriate task for the members of the house who are elected for the purpose of legislating, and that the hon. gentleman would have an opportunity when we reached the committee stage to put forward "le meilleur framjais qu'il desire dans le bill", but that there did not appear to me to be any reason why we should depart from the normal rules and, on the second reading of the bill when we are only considering the principle, seek to anticipate all the details which by our rules are taken up in committee.

For that reason, sir, it did seem to me that the amendment was not in order but, of course, I bow to the Chair in any decision.

Mr. Speaker, I think that precisely on second reading, we discuss the principle of the bill. Well, it is actually a matter of principle for us to make sure that the legislation is drafted in such a way that our Canadian citizens can understand it instead of having to come up against its ambiguous points.
That is why we submit it is actually a matter of principle that the wording of this legislation be simplified so it can be understood. Therefore, I submit that this amendment is completely in order even if it is moved at this stage.
It is unfortunate this amendment might delay the passing of Bill C-95, but I submit to you, Mr. Speaker, and to the Secretary of State, that it will take less time to have it simplified now than to wait until we are in committee where there would have to be amendments on every section, one after the other and that, in order to find a more simple wording so that every Canadian citizen can understand the act.
The trouble now is that our legislation cannot be made out, particularly the Income Tax Act. So, we might as well revise it now, at this stage, rather than wait until it is discussed in committee because that would mean longer delays in the passing of the bill.
Mr. Speaker, all I can say on the amendment moved by the hon. member for Quebec West (Mr. Plourde) is that its wording seems still more complicated than the wording of the bill in question.
So, you do not like complicated things? It was with a view to-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
The arguments which have been submitted on the point of order do not change the opinion which I had, prima facie, upon the point of order concerning the amendment proposed by the hon. member for Quebec West (Mr. Plourde). The opinion I had at the time, and which I should like to confirm now, having heard argument, is that there are certain amendments which are proposed, but which would be proposed normally in the course of the debate before the committee. I should like to cite as authority in support of this proposition Beauchesne's fourth edition, citation 390, which reads as follows:
Income Tax Act
An amendment to the second reading of a bill which covers alleged defects that can be remedied when the measure is considered in committee was ruled out by Speaker Glen on June 17, 1942, on the ground that it exceeded the limits prescribed by the rules and practice of both the United Kingdom and the Canadain House of Commons.
Then, I should like to cite May's sixteenth edition, page 531, as follows:
The amendment must not be concerned in detail with the provisions of the bill upon which it is moved, nor anticipate amendments thereto which may be moved in committee.
These two authorities confirm and substantiate the principle which I have brought to the attention of the house and which, in my opinion, show that the amendment is not in order and cannot be received at this time.

Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of privilege, and I draw to your attention standing order 12, which reads:
-in explaining a point of order or practice, he shall state the standing order-
I should like to know the number of the standing order in question.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: If the hon. member reads on the standing order, he will see that one has to state the standing order or authority. For the hon. member's information, I referred to two authorities.

Mr. Speaker, in rising to take part in this debate on second reading I must first express my appreciation of, and my sympathy with, the amendment which has just been moved. I think every one of us who has had anything to do with the Income Tax Act would dearly love to see the language simplified to a much greater extent than has hitherto been possible. I am afraid that from time to time when that has been attempted, the result has been more confusion and less clarification. At least, it is a highly desirable objective, and I should like some day to see it achieved, although frankly I doubt if that can ever be done with a taxation statute as complicated as the one with which we are dealing at the moment.
Before I start on my brief resume of the criticisms we on this side of the house may have in respect of the income tax bill, and I propose to be brief, I should like to make something very plain to the house leader with whom I have had a preliminary discussion on this matter. There are various members on this side of the house who would like to take part in this debate and who have suggested to me that they would like to speak on second reading. I know that for various reasons it is desirable to proceed with second

Income Tax Act
reading as quickly as possible. I would assume, Mr. Speaker, that we have the understanding which has prevailed heretofore, that after second reading is achieved and when the first clause is before the committee, hon. members will be given a reasonable degree of latitude to discuss the bill rather than be confined strictly to the first clause. This is, after all, a technical bill and one might enforce the technical rule that one must confine his remarks to the first clause. If that were not the case, then I can assure the house leader that various other members will be speaking on second reading. Although I can give no assurance as to what may transpire, if we have that assurance, I think as far as the official opposition is concerned we would not wish to pursue second reading much farther than it is at the moment.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I can say that I believe there has been no disposition at any stage on this side of the house to be narrowly technical about these matters. I think it has been the custom of the house, on the first clause of these important and complicated bills, to review some of the general considerations that perhaps have nothing to do directly with the principle of the bill and which hon. members want to put forward before they come to a consideration of the details of the bill. It is my understanding that neither the Minister of Finance (Mr. Gordon) nor I would be at all disposed to raise technical points of order.

Thank you; with that understanding, perhaps we can discuss for a few moments certain aspects of this measure, because before I sit down I intend to make a motion with regard to the second reading of this bill. The bill is a highly technical one and it can be considered in various ways. I propose to speak briefly because obviously if one were going to go into this matter at length, he could spend the full 40 minutes without even scratching the surface of what could be explored.
Looking at the bill in a casual way, which one must do on second reading, knowing that you are simply dealing in general with the principle, I would assume that there were perhaps four parts to it. The first, of course, would be certain technical amendments which are embodied in the bill and which I assume most members would be prepared to agree are of a technical nature, and which I am sure have been recommended by the officers of the department based on experience which has been derived in the administration of the act. I do not believe any time should be spent on a discussion of these technical amendments at this time. When we

are in the committee, of course, the technical amendments will naturally be debated and opinions expressed thereon.
Then, there is the second classification which, for lack of a better term, I can refer to as the section dealing with tax avoidance. I am not here speaking of tax evasion, but of tax avoidance. I am thinking particularly of the provision which relates to what I would call, for lack of a better term, dividend stripping, which the Minister of Finance has introduced into the bill. It gives the minister very wide powers. You will recall, Mr. Speaker, this matter was discussed at the resolution stage and some of us expressed very forcibly our opinions with respect to it. I will say that the minister has attempted to meet some of the criticisms which were raised by widening the power of appeal which was set forth in the original resolution.
With all due respect, Mr. Speaker, I say that I do not think the power of appeal goes far enough. In fact, I do not believe it is possible to draft a section to give a power of appeal where the minister exercises a discretion. Some of us are conversant with that statement which is common amongst lawyers and which came down to us over a century ago, "The devil himself knoweth not the mind of man". I am sure that no one questions the integrity of the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Garland), for whom we all have great respect and, I am sure, a great personal liking. When it comes to exercising discretion, if the Minister of National Revenue exercises his discretion honestly, and I am sure he would, then there is no appeal. The Minister of Finance has tried to rectify that by widening the power of appeal. I suggest, with all due respect, Mr. Speaker, that the amendment before us does not accomplish that purpose.
One certainly does not have to take my word for this. All he has to do is read the debate which took place at the Canadian Bar Association meeting at Banff a few short weeks ago. The opinions expressed by the tax lawyers and those who are conversant with these problems are to the effect that this is not a proper thing to do under this act. I know how complicated this problem is. I have had some experience, Mr. Speaker, in trying to deal with it myself. I suggest, with all respect, Mr. Speaker, that we do have a royal commission now dealing with the whole problem of taxation. This problem has been in existence for many years, as the minister has said. Undoubtedly, there have been abuses and perhaps the abuses have been exaggerated. However, there have been abuses; but I would suggest it would have been better for the minister to have allowed this matter to

stand until the royal commission on taxation made its report. I believe there will have to be far reaching changes made in this act. I was somewhat familiar with some of these not too many months ago. Frankly, I do not believe this is the way in which to deal with this matter. In fact, I say it is a retrograde step.
At one time, as we know, the Income Tax Act was replete with ministerial discretions. You had sections being administered by a minister or perhaps by a deputy minister, and on one occasion decisions were rendered one way and then when there was a change in personnel these sections were administered in another way. In order to eliminate this problem this parliament, not under the government of which I was a member, some years ago abolished the ministerial discretions and established an income tax appeal board. Parliament said that hereafter the Minister of National Revenue is not to exercise any discretion. Personally, after having had some little experience in office, Mr. Speaker, I think that was a proper decision, a proper attitude to take. I think this is a retrograde provision, and I would strongly urge that parliament should not enact it at this time. That is the second area.
The third area deals with tax incentives. The hon. member for Northumberland (Miss Jewett) spoke the other day at some length, and with ability and understanding of the philosophical background of tax incentives. I think that if she were starting to write the book of Genesis over again, possibly she would be right in the pronouncements she made as to how the world should be recreated. Or perhaps what the hon. member said would apply if we were in France, where you have a centrally controlled economic situation under their economic boards, or if we were even in Great Britain where the board of trade can say to a new industry, "You will locate in X city or you will not get a certificate," or "If you locate in Y city you will get nothing."
But we have not got that authoritarian control in this country. So far as this party is concerned we do not want to see that degree of control exercised by any government, and I would be very much surprised if hon. gentlemen opposite would like to see control exercised to that extent. But that was the thesis of the hon. member for Northumberland in talking about the benefits of incentives.
I say philosophically if you have the authority and this control maybe-although it is debatable from the economic standpoint -those incentives would achieve the purposes to which the hon. lady referred; but frankly I do not think in the state of our free
Income Tax Act
economy, so-called, we can expect to get the same beneficial results flowing from the incentives to which she referred.
There is another and real criticism of the incentives, and it is that they are discriminatory. Here we are on the verge of what I see as the real crux of the problem in these income tax amendments with which parliament is confronted-the discrimination between the good boys and the bad boys, the discrimination in favour of those which do achieve what the term used in the act says is a degree of Canadian ownership or a degree of Canadian control.
As I said at the outset, I do not intend to debate any of these matters at the moment. This is not the time for that. I am speaking generally now, preparatory to the motion which I propose to make before I sit down; but this is one of the problems involved in this bill, this matter of, if you have a degree of Canadian control or Canadian ownership then you are going to get a tax incentive, a write-off, or various other things. If you have not got that degree you do not get these incentives; you get some, but not others.
The Minister of Finance on that long ago night, which I am sure he would like to forget, when he first brought in his budget told us this was a budget which was going to deal primarily with employment. Does it make any great difference to a man working on a lathe whether that lathe is being operated by a Canadian company which has a degree of Canadian ownership, or whether it does not? Will his dinner pail be all the more full because he is working for one company rather than another? One could go on analysing these things, but this is not the time for such analysis. I am simply pointing out that in the incentives you have this factor of Canadian ownership, and that has particular application when you come to the area of the withholding tax.
I think that is a matter not too well recognized by our friends in the press gallery. They report very accurately when we are absent from this house and report very fully on matters and discussions vis-a-vis parties and their seating arrangements, but I noticed the other afternoon, when the Minister of Finance spoke at some length on second reading, his speech did not attract the attention it deserved. But in my opinion, and in the opinion of hon. members with whom I am associated on this side of the house, these proposals with respect to the withholding tax have a potential, most serious threat to our economy and are matters which should be considered very fully indeed before the house gives second reading to this bill.

Income Tax Act
It is true that the Minister of Finance on moving second reading the other evening gave a long list of countries to which he said there were special considerations given. And the Minister of Finance was absolutely right. You will find the list of them, or some of them at any rate, given at page 3638 of Hansard for October 16; but what the Minister of Finance did not point out-and I am sure he did it unwittingly-was the fact that these statute measures to which he referred were involved in corporation acts and were matters of incorporation and not of taxation.
I have had several letters from some of the companies to which the minister referred, some of the companies incorporated in these various countries, and all of them have asked me to ask the minister if he can name one act in which there was a discrimination vis-avis taxation rather than in the creation of the incorporation statute itself. I would ask the minister when he replies to point out any statute dealing directly with taxation in which there is a discrimination between companies which are owned by one class of citizens and companies which are owned by another class of citizens.
We are here entering into a matter of discrimination between taxpayers. As I understand the law in my not too long association with it, and after all I did practise law off and on for quite a few years-I do not recall any discriminatory tax provisions where taxpayers of one category were treated beneficially and taxpayers of another category were treated prejudicially. I do not think I can recall one at the moment, and I would like to have the minister comment on this point.
Another matter about withholding taxes to which special attention should be drawn is that the statute as we have it before us is clearly anti-American. The United States is the only country which can be affected by this income tax act as we have it at the moment, because under every other taxation agreement-and the minister can correct me if I am wrong; I do not profess to have an authoritative and detailed knowledge of every other taxation agreement-every other tax treaty we have, whether it is with Denmark, Belgium, the United Kingdom, France or any of the other countries in the world with which we have treaties, there has to be notice of abrogation. There has to be a period laid down, usually before June of one year to be effective in December the following year. The only treaty which can be abrogated by either party unilaterally is the American treaty, and that treaty says that when either party makes a tax or changes a tax, then so far as that tax is concerned the treaty is abrogated.

Therefore I am saying this is deliberately-
I will not say deliberately, but automatically 

an anti-American process, and the United States is the only country affected like this.
I would like the minister to tell us whether he has given notice of abrogation to other countries, and to tell us which countries he has given notice of abrogation to, or whether he will simply be abrogating automatically by passing this bill.
The minister may say, and I have heard this suggested in discussions in the corridors, that it is true parliament may pass the act today, the Senate may approve it today, and the Governor General give it his approval, but it does not come into effect until 1965, or at least we will not impose the tax until 1965, and we pray, hope, believe, and trust that the Americans will not take notice of it until we impose the increased tax.
That may be so, Mr. Speaker, but I think it is rather an unusual thing. I am sure no one here would realize once we pass this bill, if it is so construed, that then in any case it can be deemed to be an abrogation of the American treaty. But if it is, what happens? You get automatically a 30 per cent withholding tax. That is the tax which applies in the United States on dividends paid-30 per cent, unless there is a treaty. Although we have heard a great deal of discussion-and with this I do not quarrel- about the fact that there are American controls here and we should do something about them, and I quite agree-although I do not think it has ever yet been proven that economic penetration means political domination; that is a matter for argument-we must not forget that there happens to be a few millions of dollars invested by Canadians in the United States. And if one looks at the figures and balances the populations, which I would like to do if we were in committee, we would get an amazing result following an analysis of that picture. But in any event, what is going to happen with Canadian corporations operating in the United States?
If the 30 per cent tax comes into effect, will they have to retain very able corporation lawyers to change their corporate structure, as they easily can do, and become parents, with their Canadian companies becoming subsidiaries? This is something which can happen, and the Canadian treasury then loses the benefit of the tax and we lose control of the corporations.
This and a dozen other company questions could be raised. I am simply suggesting these as illustrations of what could be done, and why I think this question is more involved and deserves more careful consideration than what has been given to it here previously, and why we should spend more time on it,

even in the committee of the whole. This is a matter of paramount importance. This bill should be given the most careful study, and members of the House of Commons should have the benefit of the advice of experts and get the reaction of corporations and people who are going to be affected by it.
We hear a great deal about expanding our markets and our economy. Well, Mr. Speaker, where is the greatest opportunity for expansion but in the United States of America? That is the great market right next door to us, with 185 or 190 millions of population, and I suggest that for Canadian subsidiaries operating down there, and companies which I could name but which I am not going to do at the moment, their future development will be adversely affected if this bill goes into effect.
I feel very strongly that we should give careful consideration to all these matters- more, say, than has been done heretofore. One could continue at length if we were in committee, as we shall be, if the house sees fit to move into committee. But I would hope that instead of sending this bill to the committee of the whole, as would normally follow, we would send it to the committee on banking and commerce where it could be studied further and become the subject of a report from that body.
Therefore, without taking further time, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Perth:
That this bill be not now read a second time but that the subject matter relating thereto be referred to the standing committee on banking and commerce.

speakeroldname: Hon. Walter L. Gordon (Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
This, of course, is a motion in which confidence is involved and I should like to say a few words about it in replying to the remarks which have just been made by the hon. member for Digby-Annapolis-Kings (Mr. Nowlan).
To begin with, I should like to join with him in his remarks about the suggested amendment made by the hon. member for Quebec West (Mr. Plourde). I must say I sympathize with him and I agree that it would be much better if our taxing statutes were rewritten in language which the ordinary person could understand without the need for calling in tax lawyers.
Or tax consultants.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I was going to leave it at "tax lawyers". Perhaps that was a matter of personal preference. I think, though, that if the language is to be simplified, the whole act will have to be simplified and a lot of the sections in it will have to be eliminated in 28902-5-268
Income Tax Act
the interest of a simpler approach. 1 hope very much that the royal commission on taxation will be taking this matter into account in its deliberations.
I do not think I should go any further without drawing attention to the remarks which the hon. member for Digby-Annapolis-Kings made about the budget-a budget which he stated I would be very glad to forget. On the contrary, the proposals made in the budget are parts of the policy of this government which we want to see implemented just as quickly as we can.
The remaining parts?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes, the parts that are incorporated in this bill. I do not wish to be unpleasant but I do not think the hon. member for Digby-Annapolis-Kings is in a position to hold himself out as an expert in the presentation of budgets.
Much better than you are. At least, I did not bring in a rotten one.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No runs, no hits, no errors. Well, I do not want to get into controversy with the genial former minister of finance but I think, sometimes, that to do nothing is worse than anything.
The policy of your party was to keep us from doing anything.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: In moving that this bill be referred to a committee the hon. gentleman is in effect moving another motion of nonconfidence in the government.
Not necessarily.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
We shall accept it as such. At the same time, the hon. gentleman is seeking to ignore the fact that the budget itself was debated fully and at length. He is ignoring the fact that we had two votes on the budget -or three if the supply motion on July 2 is included in that category, as I think it should be. He is ignoring the detailed resolution on the income tax which was debated at length, and he is ignoring the fact that it is high time this bill was passed so that the businessmen of this country may know what the rules are going to be.
There have been 15 votes of confidence this session. I do not pose as an expert in these matters but, surely, that must be something of a record. I wonder how many more confidence motions we need to sustain the government's position.
You are calling the supply motions.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I am talking about this particular motion.
In my statement on October 6 on the second reading of this bill I said that most of

Income Tax Act
the amendments to the Income Tax Act fall into one or another of three categories. The hon. gentleman mentioned four, but one of those concerned certain very technical amendments, so I think we are both right. I do not think many hon. members would seriously question the desirability of plugging loopholes in the act. The proposed amendments which are designed for this purpose come into the first of the three categories I have mentioned. Mr. Chairman, as I understand the agreements between the Secretary of State (Mr. Pickersgill) and the spokesmen of the opposition parties, at the committee stage, and considering the nature of this bill, we can express our views on the whole of Bill C-95, without discussing it clause by clause.
Personally, I am of the opinion that this is an extremely important measure at the present time.
We heard the hon. member for Digby-Annapolis-Kings (Mr. Nowlan) making all sorts of reserves concerning the bill under study, claiming that we should be very cautious, that the directors of foreign businesses having capital in Canadian industry should not be offended.
Mr. Chairman, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Gordon) was quite right when he stated, the other day, that the time for speeches is over, that action is what is now required. To my mind, Bill C-95 clearly establishes that the present government intends to act in a positive way, and to find some concrete remedies.
We all know that today, this country's-economy is impaired by the fact that 60 per cent of the Canadian manufacturing industry are controlled by non-resident corporations. We must hand back to Canadians the ownership and control of their own economy.
Bill C-95 aims to put back that control of industries into the hands of Canadian citizens, by altering the rates of the withholding tax on dividends of non-resident corporations; the rate would be reduced from 15 to 10 per cent for corporations which will allow Canadians to buy their shares and to sit on their boards of directors.
In order to reach our economic aim, it is essential that Canadians have a voice on the boards of directors within Canadian industry. I congratulate the Minister of Finance for taking concrete steps to promote this repatriation of Canadian interests into the hands of Canadians.

Income Tax Act
As for those executives who do not want to have Canadians on their boards, well, they will have to pay a higher rate on dividends payable by a non-resident person, as the rate will be increased from 15 to 20 per cent.
Mr. Chairman, I am of the opinion that this bill is extremely important and represents a turning point in the history of Canada as far as taxation is concerned.
It was necessary to act quickly, and I congratulate the government for taking a bold stand in order to encourage industrialists who have invested in Canada to let Canadians have a say on their boards, so that they can have the share which must be theirs in foreign trade.
Mr. Chairman, we all know that the main economic problem now facing Canada is our unfavourable trade balance with the United States. I feel we must tackle the problem energetically, as we are doing at present.
We agree that our aim will not be easily achieved, but we feel that those industrialists will understand the situation if we clearly explain our intentions to them. As a result, in a more or less distant future, 25 per cent of the shareholders and directors of the companies which develop our natural resources will be Canadians.
I submit that this bill will be most useful in that connection and that we will have to adopt similar legislation to increase our trade with the United States so as to remove, as it were, our present trade deficit.
We will then no longer have to stand the unending pressures of American industrialists on our Canadian economy.
Mr. Chairman, the second point I wish to discuss is the review of our whole taxation structures. I gather that the royal commission on taxation is still proceeding with its work, but we all earnestly hope that it will soon submit its report to the house, so that we may be able to overhaul our taxation system. Actually, it is so complicated that it is unfair to salaried workers or owners of small businesses who have no experts at their disposal to take advantage of all the benefits which they could claim under certain provisions of the statute.
I feel that the Minister of Finance is making a concrete gesture in introducing Bill No. C-95.
In fact, he is endeavouring to eliminate certain loopholes that manufacturers or financiers could find in the legislation.
Let us consider, for example, the question of lease-purchase option agreements, where, of course the treasury could be deprived of huge amounts. Surely, we did not have to wait for royal commissions' reports or exten-

sive studies to eliminate such loopholes. In fact, I think that it was up to the minister to act promptly, and he has done so by introducing Bill No. C-95.
Mr. Chairman, I think that the aims of the provisions contained in Bill No. C-95 are excellent. Let us take, for example, the concealment of dividends which is commonly known as "dividend stripping".
Those people have tried everything and even though it may be at times distasteful to give too much discretion to the Minister of Finance and to the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Garland), I think that we should consider first and above all the nation's interest and endeavour to prevent people from cheating the Department of National Revenue, so that all classes of society will pay the government what the government is entitled to. We have to do it, even though certain methods might be distasteful at times; but if they prove inefficient, the government has to step in once more and to introduce new legislation, so as to do justice to every taxpayer.
Personally, I represent a riding where the unemployment situation is extremely serious, and it is with infinite pleasure that I welcomed the announcement of the Minister of Labour (Mr. MacEachen) and the Minister of Industry (Mr. Drury) with regard to designated areas, in which the county of St. Maurice-Lafleche has been included.
A point of great account, which it is extremely important to recall in the house, is that out of 66 designated areas recognized by the Department of Labour, 30 are located in the province of Quebec, which means that Quebec is the province which suffers most from unemployment in this country. It also proves that the Liberal government realized that the economic problem in the province of Quebec had to be solved. We have here some positive action, which the members from the province of Quebec should bring to the attention of the house.
It could, perhaps, be said that the legislation is discriminatory. The point has already been raised, and much fuss has been made of the case of Brantford. But none the less, it is an extremely important legislation and a most practical one, which tends to solve the unemployment problem and also the problem of Quebec's economy, where all industrial strength is practically centralized in the Montreal area, the other parts of the province having to bear the consequences of such a situation.
Thanks to this new legislation, several areas in the province of Quebec may, from now on, offer some advantage to industry, whereas they were unable to do so in the past.

Let us take, for instance, the benefits offered to the industrialists by the Minister of Industry and by the Minister of Finance, that is a tax abatement for a three year period and the possibility of a deduction for machinery and buildings over a five year period.
I think those measures ought to prompt industries to set up in the areas where unfortunately the economic situation is not favourable.
In the riding which I represent, we experienced a tremendous economic development in the years 1925-30 because at that time, we had electric power which was the key to our economy; but since the nationalization of electric power, that power can be found everywhere in the province of Quebec, and our region lost the advantages it had before.
Because of this new legislation, we hope that the industries will come and set up in our region where economic growth is very slow. I think that this legislation is not discriminatory, that it is in order and serves the interests of the nation. As was mentioned by the hon. member for Northumberland (Miss Jewett), this legislation was implemented in other countries and it gave satisfactory results.
I therefore think it is by duty to point out that this legislation is intended to decentralize industry and promote the most severely affected regions.
As regards the methods used for the designation of those places, they may come under criticism. But if we take a map and study the economic divisions where development is too slow, we find that, actually, the places which suffer the most economically in Canada will benefit from those advantages. Therefore, people should not complain about the procedure followed.
Some complaints have been heard that the municipalities and the provinces have not been consulted. In fact, it might be advisable to examine the matter more carefully in this respect. Obviously, the machinery is perhaps not yet sufficiently to the point; therefore, it is important to name a standing committee on federal-provincial relations, which would prevent interference in a field where there may be competition between the provinces and the federal government.
However, even if such a problem has been raised, this is no reason to stop the whole legislation. On the contrary, we should act. If there are abuses they should be remedied but we should not refrain from taking action because a constitutional problem may arise.
Everyone should take his own responsibilities and, in this, the government is acting quite properly.

I should like to come back to the excellent suggestion made by the hon. member for Lake St. John (Mr. Lessard) concerning the possibility of eliminating receipts for charitable donations and reducing from 17 to 14 or 15 per cent the tax levied at the present time on the first bracket of taxable income. Another suggestion would be to raise the tax basis in such a way that the national revenue would not lose anything and taxpayers would not have to keep on fighting with the officers

oi the Department of National Revenue, thereby doing away with a practice which could be called a premium on charity.
If we are generous, we will get our reward at the end of our life on earth.
I am of the opinion that the Minister of Finance should examine those suggestions with care, for I am sure there are ways to improve the situation. Maybe there have been excesses, but the situation must be corrected. Mr. Chairman, I am pleased to take part in the debate on Bill C-95.
This bill includes many things, but we would have liked it to bring forward some relief to the Canadian people. Unfortunately, taxpayers will not be helped by it. It can be noted that tax exemptions are very few. In fact, there are only a few changes, a few amendments to the various clauses which, on the whole, merely move things from one place to another.
Mr. Chairman, our society is disintegrating and we are too blind to realize it. We can judge of the soundness of society only by the wealth we have gathered. As long as we do not see sticks and clubs, we will remain very quiet, like the Bourbons of Spain a few centuries ago.
I am convinced that Bill C-95 could be improved.
Aware of our duties and obligations toward society, we claim a $3,000 income tax exemption for bachelors. In my opinion, that should be included in the bill. Married taxpayers should enjoy a $5,000 exemption, plus a $1,000 exemption for each child. Unfortunately, this is not in the bill.
Also, we claim a tax deduction on all workmen's tools used by their owners to earn their living. We should also have liked students to benefit from a tax exemption on their tuition fees. A family head should be allowed to deduct from his income tax the tuition fees for his children aged 16 and over. Unfortunately, there is no mention of those exemptions in the bill.
The government does not know where to get the money. That is why it is seeking means to replenish the treasury. I know that the government needs money and that it must find it somewhere. An easy solution would be to reduce the interest rates and to use the facilities of the Bank of Canada to finance public works. That would be two ways for the government to secure the necessary funds without cost. We could use that institution to achieve that end if we wanted to, but unfortunately it is impossible under

the present financial system. It is felt that the Bank of Canada should not be put at the disposal of the Canadian people, but where is the money going to come from?
But I would ask the Minister of Finance to look for money where he can find it.
If you refuse to do so, if you have to steal money from the workers in order to give it to the needy, at least be wise enough to take it from those who benefit most from society. At least, leave what is necessary to those who need it to live decently.
Allow me, Mr. Chairman, to quote a few statistics in support of my remarks.
On page 1039 of the Canada Year Book for
1962,	we find that individuals pay the same amount in taxes as companies and their shareholders. Why must they always be granted exemptions that enable them to pile up profits and capital at the expense of other people who are always in debt and have no security?
It was announced that the period between August 1962 and August 1963 would be a year of austerity for all Canada, and special personal income taxes were levied. During the period between August 1962 and August
1963,	the market value of the shares of 740 companies or trusts increased from $44,740,769,022 to $57,351,895,062, that is by almost $13 billion. For whom were the austerity measures meant? And companies are always complaining that their profits are too low, that they fear the future and that they need tax relief in order to survive. What about the private individual?
Do you know that, in 1962, the Canadian taxpayer paid $700 out of his income solely for the administration of the federal government, that is almost 44 per cent of the average salary?
Do you know that interest charges take between 16 and 17 cents out of each tax dollar, and they keep increasing. It is not surprising that Khrushchev claims that communism will one day overcome capitalism.
Do you know that federal and provincial taxes have increased by 3,000 per cent during the last 50 years?
It is unthinkable that a country as highly industrialized as ours, with a large and hardworking labour force with a sufficient number of technicians, experts and engineers, should find itself at the mercy of such an extent that it is virtually enslaved by financial and economical means.
We have no one to blame but ourselves, and our irresponsible governments. Our industries must increase their output, widen their fields of production in order to be in a position to employ all the available manpower and raise our standard of living.

I move, seconded by the hon. member for St. Boniface (Mr. Teillet):
That the special committee on procedures and organization of the House of Commons appointed October 23, 1963, be composed of Mr. Speaker and
Business of the House Messrs. Aiken, Chapdelaine, Choquette, Gregoire, Jewett (Miss), Knowles, Lambert, Lamoureux, Mac-Eachen, Macquarrie, Martineau, Pickersgill, Walker, Woolliams.
Motion agreed to.
I presume the order of business for tomorrow is that outlined by the house leader yesterday?

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Yes. Perhaps I should make provision for the contingency tomorrow evening. If, as I hope will be the case, we have disposed of the bill in committee by five o'clock we will take the estimates of northern affairs tomorrow evening. If, however, we go on as far as eight o'clock before we get into committee of supply, we would take the estimates of the Department of Fisheries and try to finish them. Of course, if we do not finish until 10.30 we will not be able to take the estimates of either department.
And you will go on with the bill on Friday?

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Yes, of course. If perchance this bill is not disposed of tomorrow we will go on with it on Friday.

It being three minutes after six o'clock the house adjourned, without question put.

Thursday, October 31, 1963
